text: Mac Conglinne was an Irish hero of satire, not a mythological character. He had a vision in a 12th-century Irish aisling poem. The poor bard came from County Roscommon and went on a poet's circuit of the province of Munster. There he heard that poets were treated well, but the king suffered from uncontrollable gluttony. In Cork he received no welcome. He was put in a dingy hovel where fleas and lice ate him alive. Furious, he composed a satire so scathing that the abbot condemned him to be crucified. The night before his execution he was tied to a stone like the great hero Cúchulainn. An angel recited a long poem describing a land made entirely of food. Mac Conglinne knew this vision was the secret to restore the gluttonous king. He recited the vision before the manacled king, who vomited a demon from his mouth. The demon grabbed some of the food and disappeared. The satire blends beliefs in hospitality and the prestige of the poet with folkloric monsters that can possess bodies.

okr.objective: Document Mac Conglinne as an Irish satire hero whose vision restores a gluttonous king.
